The Keyless Pipeline

How a React app gets from git push on your laptop to running pods on AWS EKS — automatically, in about ten minutes, with no AWS password, key, or token stored anywhere. Written for people who have never touched a pipeline before.

01  What this is

Read this first. Everything else is detail.

This repository holds the frontend of an AI Interview Platform: the part that runs in a person's browser. It is a React application — a folder of JavaScript files that gets compiled into plain HTML, CSS and JS, then served by a small web server called nginx.

On its own, that is unremarkable. What this repository is really about is everything that happens after you type git push: the code is checked, tested, scanned for secrets and known vulnerabilities, packed into a container image, pushed to Amazon's private registry, and rolled out onto a Kubernetes cluster running in AWS — without a human touching a server, and without a single AWS credential being written down anywhere.

The one idea to take away

A pipeline that stores an AWS access key is a pipeline with a permanent liability sitting in it. This one has none. GitHub proves who it is with a signed, expiring token, AWS checks that proof against a rule it holds, and hands back credentials that die within the hour. Nothing to leak, nothing to rotate, nothing to forget.

The vocabulary, in one table

If some of the words below are new, that is expected. Skim this now and come back to the glossary whenever a term stops making sense.

WordWhat it actually means here
CIContinuous Integration — every push gets built and tested automatically, so a broken change is caught in minutes rather than at release time.
CDContinuous Deployment — if the checks pass on master, the change goes live on its own. No ticket, no manual copy.
ContainerYour app plus everything it needs to run, sealed into one file. It behaves the same on your laptop and in AWS.
ImageThe sealed file itself. A running copy of an image is a container.
Registry (ECR)A private warehouse for images inside your AWS account.
KubernetesThe system that runs containers across many machines, restarts them when they die, and replaces them one at a time during an update.
EKSKubernetes, operated by AWS so you don't have to run the control plane yourself.
IAMAWS's permission system: who is allowed to do what.
OIDCThe trust mechanism that lets GitHub prove its identity to AWS without a shared password.

PathRole

02  The whole flow

.github/workflows/ci.yml

One push starts four jobs. Three of them run at the same time and check different things. The fourth — the one that touches AWS — only starts if all three came back green, and only on the master branch.

Reading the diagram in plain words

  1. You push a commit, or open a pull request.
  2. GitHub starts a fresh, empty Ubuntu machine (a runner) and runs three jobs on it in parallel.
  3. app installs dependencies, checks code style, runs tests with coverage, builds the bundle, and uploads the result to SonarCloud.
  4. secrets scans the entire git history for anything that looks like a password or key.
  5. manifests checks the Kubernetes YAML against the real Kubernetes schemas, so a typo is caught before the cluster sees it.
  6. If any of those fail, the run stops. Nothing is built, nothing is deployed.
  7. If all three pass and the branch is master, the deploy job starts. It asks GitHub for an identity token, trades it with AWS for temporary credentials, scans the image, pushes it, applies it to the cluster, and waits for the new pods to be healthy.
  8. If the rollout stalls or the smoke test fails, it undoes the rollout automatically and prints why.
Why parallel, then a gate

Running the three checks at the same time means feedback in about three minutes instead of nine. Making the deploy job needs: [app, secrets, manifests] means speed never costs you safety — the fast path still cannot skip a single check.

03  The toolbox

Every tool this project uses, what it is, and where it appears

Twenty-two moving parts sounds like a lot. It isn't, once you see that each one answers exactly one question. Grouped below by the question they answer.

Build — "how does source become a website?"

React 18 The UI library. You describe what the screen should look like for a given state; React updates the browser to match. src/ · pages, components, hooks
Vite 6 The build tool. Runs a fast dev server while you work, and compiles everything into a small dist/ folder for production. vite.config.js · npm run dev / build
Node.js 22 The JavaScript runtime that Vite, ESLint and the tests run on. It exists only at build time — the shipped image has no Node in it. actions/setup-node · Dockerfile build stage
npm & the lockfile npm ci installs exactly the versions written in package-lock.json and fails if they don't match — so CI builds what you tested. package-lock.json · npm ci

Quality — "is this code any good?"

ESLint 9 Reads the code without running it and flags mistakes and bad patterns. Configured with --max-warnings 0: even a warning fails the build. eslint.config.js · npm run lint
Vitest + Testing Library Runs unit tests in a simulated browser (jsdom) and measures how much of the code they touched. src/test/ · npm run test:coverage
SonarCloud Hosted static analysis. Tracks bugs, code smells, duplication and coverage over time, and comments on pull requests. sonar-project.properties · SONAR_TOKEN

Security — "what could hurt us?"

Gitleaks Scans the entire git history for committed secrets — AWS keys, tokens, private keys. Deleting a secret in a later commit does not hide it; Gitleaks still finds it. ci.yml · job: secrets · fetch-depth: 0
Trivy Scans the built image for known vulnerabilities. Set to fail on CRITICAL only, ignoring issues with no fix available yet. ci.yml · runs before the ECR push
kubeconform Validates the Kubernetes YAML against the official schemas in strict mode, so an unknown field or a typo fails in CI rather than on the cluster. ci.yml · job: manifests
OpenID Connect (OIDC) The reason there is no AWS key in this repo. GitHub issues a short-lived signed token; AWS verifies it and hands back temporary credentials. permissions: id-token: write

Package — "how do we ship it?"

Docker Builds the image. This one is multi-stage: a Node stage compiles the app, and only the compiled files are copied into the final image. Dockerfile · .dockerignore
nginx The web server inside the image. Serves the files on port 3000, answers /healthz, sets cache and security headers, and falls back to index.html for client-side routes. nginx.conf
Alpine Linux The tiny base OS both stages build on. Fewer packages means a smaller image and a smaller attack surface for Trivy to find problems in. node:22-alpine · nginx:alpine

Automation — "who does all this, and when?"

GitHub Hosts the code, the pull requests, the encrypted secrets, and the production environment that guards the deploy job. github.com/vikki-iam/eks-demo
GitHub Actions The CI/CD engine. Reads ci.yml, starts clean virtual machines, runs the jobs, and throws the machines away afterwards. .github/workflows/ci.yml

Cloud — "where does it actually run?"

AWS The cloud account everything lives in. Region ap-south-1 (Mumbai). env.AWS_REGION
IAM AWS's permission system. Holds the role the pipeline assumes and the trust policy that decides which GitHub workflow is allowed to assume it. secrets.AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN
STS Security Token Service — the AWS service that inspects GitHub's token and issues the temporary credentials. Nothing it returns lives longer than the job. AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
Amazon ECR The private image registry. Every image is tagged with the exact commit SHA, so you can always tell which line of code is running. ai-interview-dev-platform/frontend
Amazon EKS Managed Kubernetes. AWS runs the control plane; your pods run on the worker nodes. cluster: ai-interview
Kubernetes objects Deployment (how many copies, which image), Service (a stable address), ConfigMap (non-secret settings). k8s/deployment.yaml, service.yaml, configmap.yaml
kubectl The command-line client for Kubernetes. The pipeline uses it to apply the manifests, watch the rollout, verify, and undo. ci.yml · deploy steps

04  No hardcoded credentials

The part that matters most — read it twice

To deploy to AWS, something has to prove it is allowed to. The obvious way is to create an AWS user, generate an access key, and paste it into GitHub. Millions of pipelines do exactly that. It works, and it is the single most common way cloud accounts get taken over.

The problem is not that the key is weak. It is that the key exists at rest: written into a settings page, copied into someone's notes, present in a backup, valid at 3 a.m. six months after the person who made it left. A secret that never expires is a secret you will eventually lose track of.

How the exchange actually works

OIDC (OpenID Connect) is the same idea as "Sign in with Google", turned around. GitHub acts as the identity provider. AWS is told, once, "I trust tokens signed by GitHub" — and then, more importantly, "but only if the token says it came from this repository."

What makes this repository ask for a token

Exactly one line. Without it the runner has no way to request a token at all, and step 1 above fails:

.github/workflows/ci.yml — deploy job 
# The default for the whole workflow is read-only:
permissions:
  contents: read

# ...and only the deploy job widens it, by one permission:
jobs:
  deploy:
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write   # ← lets this job request an OIDC token. Nothing more.
A common misreading

id-token: write does not grant any access to AWS. It only permits the job to ask GitHub for a signed statement of identity. Whether that statement is worth anything is decided entirely on the AWS side, by the trust policy.

The one AWS-side rule

This is the trust policy attached to the IAM role. Read the Condition block closely — it is the fence around your AWS account:

IAM role → Trust relationships 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {
      // The OIDC provider you registered once, in this account
      "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
    },
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
    "Condition": {
      "StringEquals": {
        // Who the token is for. Must be AWS, or a token meant for
        // some other service could be replayed here.
        "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com",

        // Who the token is from. This job declares `environment: production`,
        // so GitHub sets the subject to the environment form — NOT the branch form.
        "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:vikki-iam/eks-demo:environment:production"
      }
    }
  }]
}
The trap that catches almost everyone

GitHub changes the sub claim depending on how the job is written. A job with no environment gets repo:OWNER/REPO:ref:refs/heads/master. A job that declares environment: production — as this one does — gets repo:OWNER/REPO:environment:production instead. Copy the wrong form into the trust policy and every deploy fails with Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, with nothing in the message to tell you why.

Never write this

A trust policy with "sub": "repo:vikki-iam/*", or with the sub condition missing entirely, will happily accept a token from a fork, from a pull request, or from an unrelated repository. Pin the full string. If you need more than one branch or environment, use StringLike with an explicit pattern — never a bare wildcard.

So what is stored in GitHub?

Two values, and neither is an AWS credential:

SecretWhat it isIs it a credential?
AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN The name of the role to assume, e.g. arn:aws:iam::123…:role/gh-deploy-frontend. Knowing it grants nothing — you still need a token that satisfies the trust policy. No — stored as a secret only to keep the account ID out of logs
SONAR_TOKEN Upload token for SonarCloud, scoped to that one project. Not an AWS thing at all. Yes, but for SonarCloud only
GITHUB_TOKEN Created and destroyed by GitHub for each run. You never see it or set it. Automatic — expires with the job

The rest of the no-secrets discipline

  • No API URL baked into the bundle. The frontend reads its configuration at container start, not at build time — see section 08.
  • No .env in git. .gitignore excludes .env and .env.*.local; only .env.example, which contains no real values, is committed.
  • Nothing secret in a ConfigMap. Everything in k8s/configmap.yaml is served to every visitor's browser anyway. Secrets would belong in a Kubernetes Secret backed by AWS Secrets Manager — not here.
  • Gitleaks scans the full history (fetch-depth: 0), so a secret committed months ago and deleted last week is still caught.
  • The pipeline never prints a credential. The AWS action masks what it receives, and the deploy summary shows only the commit, image tag, cluster and namespace.

05  Stage by stage

.github/workflows/ci.yml, top to bottom

The numbers below are a real sequence: each stage only happens because the one before it succeeded. Stages 03–08 are the three parallel jobs; everything from 09 onwards is the deploy job.

  1. 01

    The trigger

    on: · concurrency:

    The workflow starts on a push to main or master, on any pull request, or when someone clicks "Run workflow" in the Actions tab. 

    on:
  push:
    branches: [main, master]
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  group: ci-frontend-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}

    Concurrency means: if you push twice quickly to the same pull request, the older run is cancelled — nobody cares about results for code you already replaced. On master it is deliberately not cancelled, because a half-finished deploy is worse than a slow one.

  2. 02

    Check out and install

    job: app · ~40 s

    A clean Ubuntu machine downloads the code and installs Node 22. npm ci — not npm install — installs precisely the versions in package-lock.json and errors out if the lockfile and package.json disagree. That is what makes two runs of the same commit produce the same build. 

    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  with: { fetch-depth: 0 }      # full history — Sonar and Gitleaks need it
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
  with: { node-version: "22", cache: npm }
- run: npm ci
  3. 03

    Lint

    npm run lint → eslint . --max-warnings 0

    ESLint reads the code without running it. The --max-warnings 0 flag is the opinionated bit: warnings are treated as failures, so the codebase never accumulates a backlog of "we'll fix it later" that everybody learns to ignore.

  4. 04

    Test, with coverage

    npm run test:coverage → vitest run --coverage

    Tests run in jsdom, a fake browser, so React components can be rendered and clicked without opening a real one. Coverage is written as lcov for Sonar to read. 

    // vite.config.js
coverage: {
  provider: 'v8',
  reporter: ['text', 'lcov'],
  all: true,               // count every file under src/, not just imported ones
  include: ['src/**/*.{js,jsx}'],
}

    all: true matters more than it looks. Without it, a file with no tests is simply absent from the report — so deleting a test would raise your coverage number. With it, untested files count as zero, which is the truth.

  5. 05

    Build

    npm run build → vite build → dist/

    Vite compiles React into plain files a browser understands, splits vendor code into separate chunks (react, mui) so a small app change doesn't invalidate every browser cache, and writes source maps for debugging.

  6. 06

    SonarCloud analysis

    SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action@v8.2.1

    Uploads the source and the coverage report to SonarCloud, which tracks bugs, code smells, duplication and coverage across time and comments on pull requests. 

    sonar.projectKey=vikki-iam_eks-demo
sonar.organization=vikki-iam
sonar.sources=src
sonar.tests=src/test
sonar.javascript.lcov.reportPaths=coverage/lcov.info
  7. 07

    Secret scan

    job: secrets · gitleaks/gitleaks-action@v2

    Runs in parallel with everything above. Gitleaks walks the full commit history looking for anything shaped like a credential. Because git keeps every version of every file forever, a secret that was committed and then "removed" is still sitting there — this is the job that finds it.

    It has pull-requests: write so it can post its findings on the PR, and nothing else.

  8. 08

    Manifest validation

    job: manifests · kubeconform v0.6.7

    Checks the three YAML files in k8s/ against the official Kubernetes schemas in -strict mode, which rejects unknown fields. A misspelled contaienrPort would otherwise be silently ignored by the cluster and you would debug a service that never gets traffic. 

    - uses: docker://ghcr.io/yannh/kubeconform:v0.6.7
  with:
    args: -strict -summary k8s/configmap.yaml k8s/service.yaml k8s/deployment.yaml
  9. 09

    The gate

    job: deploy · needs · if · environment

    Four independent conditions have to line up before anything touches AWS:

    needs: [app, secrets, manifests]      # all three checks passed

if: >-
  github.ref == 'refs/heads/master' &&    # master only
  (github.event_name == 'push' || github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch')

environment:
  name: production                   # optional approvals + scoped secrets

concurrency:
  group: deploy-frontend
  cancel-in-progress: false           # never interrupt a live rollout

    A pull request from a fork therefore cannot deploy, cannot read the production secrets, and cannot request a token that the trust policy would accept — three separate reasons, any one of which would be enough.

    Before doing anything else the job asserts its own configuration is present, so a missing secret fails in five seconds with a clear message instead of halfway through a deploy: 

    - name: Check config
  run: |
    for v in AWS_REGION EKS_CLUSTER K8S_NAMESPACE ECR_REPO ROLE_ARN; do
      [ -z "${!v}" ] && echo "::error::$v is not set" && missing=1
    done
  10. 10

    Log in to AWS — without a password

    aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4

    This is the exchange drawn in section 04. Note what is absent: no aws-access-key-id, no aws-secret-access-key. 

    - name: Log in to AWS
  uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
  with:
    role-to-assume: ${{ secrets.AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN }}
    role-session-name: gh-deploy-frontend   # shows up in CloudTrail
    aws-region: ${{ env.AWS_REGION }}

    role-session-name is worth setting properly: every AWS API call this job makes is recorded in CloudTrail under that name, so an audit can tie a cluster change back to a specific pipeline rather than to "someone".

  11. 11

    Build the image, then scan it

    docker build · aquasecurity/trivy-action@v0.36.0

    The image is built and scanned before it is pushed. A vulnerable image therefore never reaches the registry at all, so nobody can pull it by accident later. 

    - run: docker build -t scan-target .

- uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@v0.36.0
  with:
    image-ref: scan-target
    severity: CRITICAL         # fail only on the worst class
    ignore-unfixed: true       # don't block on CVEs with no patch yet
    exit-code: '1'             # ← without this, findings are printed and ignored
    Read that last line again

    A scanner without exit-code: '1' is decoration. It prints a nice table, the step goes green, and the vulnerable image ships anyway. The exit code is what turns a report into a gate.

  12. 12

    Push to ECR

    aws-actions/amazon-ecr-login@v2

    The ECR login action uses the temporary credentials from stage 10 to fetch a short-lived docker login. The image is tagged with the full commit SHA — never latest. 

    IMAGE=$REGISTRY/$ECR_REPO/frontend:$SHA
docker tag scan-target "$IMAGE"
docker push "$IMAGE"

    Tagging by commit means you can look at a running pod, read its image tag, and go straight to the exact line of code. latest gives you none of that and makes rollback ambiguous.

  13. 13

    Deploy to EKS

    aws eks update-kubeconfig · kubectl apply

    update-kubeconfig writes a temporary kubeconfig that authenticates to the cluster using the same short-lived credentials — still nothing stored. Then the manifests are applied, with the image substituted in. 

    # fail loudly if the placeholder is gone, rather than deploying a literal string
grep -q IMAGE_PLACEHOLDER k8s/deployment.yaml || exit 1

kubectl apply -n "$K8S_NAMESPACE" -f k8s/configmap.yaml -f k8s/service.yaml
sed "s|IMAGE_PLACEHOLDER|$IMAGE|" k8s/deployment.yaml | kubectl apply -n "$K8S_NAMESPACE" -f -
kubectl rollout status deployment/frontend -n "$K8S_NAMESPACE" --timeout=5m

    rollout status is the step that turns "the YAML was accepted" into "the new pods are actually running and healthy". Without it, the job would go green the moment Kubernetes acknowledged the request, whether or not the container ever started.

  14. 14

    Verify from inside the cluster

    kubectl run … curlimages/curl

    A throwaway pod is started inside the namespace and asked to fetch the site through the Service. This proves the whole chain works — Service selector, pod readiness, nginx, the files themselves — not just that a container is alive. 

    kubectl run "verify-fe-${SHA:0:8}-${GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT}" \
  --rm --attach --restart=Never -q \
  -n "$K8S_NAMESPACE" --image=curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -- \
  -fsS --max-time 10 http://frontend/ -o /dev/null

    The pod name includes the commit and the attempt number so a retry doesn't collide with the leftover pod from the previous try.

  15. 15

    Roll back and report

    if: failure() · kubectl rollout undo

    If the rollout stalled or the verification failed, the job undoes the rollout by itself and then dumps the pod list and the tail of describe — usually enough to see the cause without opening a terminal. 

    - name: Roll back
  if: failure() && (steps.deploy.outcome == 'success' || steps.deploy.outcome == 'failure')
  run: |
    kubectl rollout undo deployment/frontend -n "$K8S_NAMESPACE" || true
    kubectl rollout status deployment/frontend -n "$K8S_NAMESPACE" --timeout=3m || true
    kubectl get pods -n "$K8S_NAMESPACE" -l app=frontend
    kubectl describe pods -n "$K8S_NAMESPACE" -l app=frontend | tail -30

    Finally, every run — pass or fail — writes a small table to the GitHub run summary with the commit, image, cluster and namespace, so you never have to expand log groups to find out what was deployed.

06  Security gates

Six checks, each able to stop the run on its own

A "gate" is a check with teeth: if it fails, the pipeline stops. A check that only prints a warning is a report, not a gate. Every one of the six below is wired to fail the run.

GateCatchesRuns onHow it fails the run
Gitleaks AWS keys, tokens, private keys committed anywhere in history every push and PR non-zero exit from the action
ESLint unused variables, broken hooks rules, unsafe patterns every push and PR --max-warnings 0
Vitest behaviour regressions; produces the coverage report every push and PR any failing test
SonarCloud bugs, code smells, duplication, coverage trend every push and PR quality gate status (configure it in SonarCloud)
kubeconform invalid or misspelled Kubernetes manifests every push and PR -strict rejects unknown fields
Trivy known CRITICAL vulnerabilities in the OS and libraries in the image deploy job, before the push exit-code: '1'

The gates you can't see

Four more controls do not appear as steps, but do as much work as the ones that do:

  • Default-deny token permissions. The workflow starts at contents: read. If someone injects a malicious step, it cannot push code, open a release, or touch issues, because the token it would steal has no such rights.
  • Branch and event conditions. Deployment is impossible from a branch that is not master, and from an event that is not a push or a manual dispatch.
  • The production environment. Deploy-scoped secrets live behind it, and you can add required reviewers there without touching the workflow file at all.
  • The OIDC trust policy. Even if every other control were bypassed, AWS still refuses a token whose sub is not exactly this repository's production environment.

07  IAM & least privilege

What the pipeline is allowed to do — and nothing more

"Least privilege" means the deploy role can do exactly the handful of things this pipeline needs and would be useless to anyone who somehow got hold of it. The permissions split in two, because Kubernetes has its own permission system layered on top of AWS's.

Layer 1 — the AWS permissions policy

Attached to the role, this is what the temporary credentials can do:

IAM role → Permissions 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      // Getting a registry login token can only be granted account-wide;
      // by itself it lets you log in, not read or write any repository.
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "ecr:GetAuthorizationToken",
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      // Push and pull, scoped to this one repository.
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability",
        "ecr:InitiateLayerUpload",
        "ecr:UploadLayerPart",
        "ecr:CompleteLayerUpload",
        "ecr:PutImage",
        "ecr:BatchGetImage"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:ecr:ap-south-1:<ACCOUNT_ID>:repository/ai-interview-dev-platform/frontend"
    },
    {
      // Only enough to build a kubeconfig for this one cluster.
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "eks:DescribeCluster",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:eks:ap-south-1:<ACCOUNT_ID>:cluster/ai-interview"
    }
  ]
}
What is deliberately missing

No ecr:DeleteRepository, no iam:*, no ec2:*, no eks:UpdateClusterConfig, no access to any other ECR repository or cluster. If this role were somehow assumed by an attacker, the worst they could do is push an image to one repository and read one cluster's description.

Layer 2 — permission inside the cluster

eks:DescribeCluster lets you build a kubeconfig; it does not let you use it. Kubernetes decides that separately. On a modern EKS cluster you grant it with an access entry: 

# 1. tell the cluster this IAM role maps to a Kubernetes identity
aws eks create-access-entry \
  --cluster-name ai-interview \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:role/gh-deploy-frontend \
  --type STANDARD

# 2. give that identity admin rights in ONE namespace only
aws eks associate-access-policy \
  --cluster-name ai-interview \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:role/gh-deploy-frontend \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:eks::aws:cluster-access-policy/AmazonEKSAdminPolicy \
  --access-scope type=namespace,namespaces=demo

type=namespace,namespaces=demo is the important part: the pipeline is an admin of the demo namespace and a nobody everywhere else in the cluster.

Older clusters

If the cluster still uses the aws-auth ConfigMap instead of access entries, the equivalent is a mapRoles entry pointing at a Role/RoleBinding you create in the demo namespace. Prefer access entries on anything new — a mistake in aws-auth can lock everyone out of the cluster.

The GitHub side of least privilege

ScopePermissionWhy
whole workflowcontents: readthe floor for every job: read the code, nothing else
job: secretspull-requests: writeso Gitleaks can comment findings on the PR
job: deployid-token: writeso it can request an OIDC token — the only job that can

Three jobs out of four cannot request a token at all. That is not a formality: it means a compromised dependency in the test suite has no path to AWS, because the machinery it would need is not enabled in that job.

08  Config without secrets

src/config.js · docker-entrypoint.sh · k8s/configmap.yaml

A frontend needs to know where its API lives. The tempting approach is to put the URL in an environment variable at build time — but a frontend build bakes that value into the JavaScript. One value per build means one image per environment, which means the image you tested in dev is not the image you ship to production. You are then testing something you never deploy.

This project builds the image once and configures it at start-up instead.

How the value reaches the browser

Three short hops, and nothing sensitive at any of them:

1 — k8s/configmap.yaml → environment variables in the pod 
envFrom:
  - configMapRef:
      name: frontend-config
2 — docker-entrypoint.sh → a small JS file, written at start 
// escaped so a quote or backslash in a value cannot break out of the
// string and inject code into every page load
cat > /usr/share/nginx/html/runtime-config.js <<EOF
window.__APP_CONFIG__ = {
  apiBaseUrl: "$(escape_js "${API_BASE_URL}")",
  appEnv:     "$(escape_js "${APP_ENV}")"
};
EOF

exec "$@"   # nginx becomes PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly
3 — src/config.js → what the app reads 
const runtime = typeof window !== 'undefined' ? window.__APP_CONFIG__ || {} : {};

export const config = {
  apiBaseUrl: (runtime.apiBaseUrl || '').replace(/\/+$/, ''),
  appEnv:     runtime.appEnv || 'dev',
  apiPrefix:  '/api/v1',
};
Why this is safe

Everything in runtime-config.js is downloaded by every visitor, so it must contain nothing you would not print on a billboard: an API URL and an environment name. Real secrets never go near a browser — they belong to the backend, which reads them from a Kubernetes Secret or AWS Secrets Manager.

Behaviour worth knowing

Editing the ConfigMap alone does not restart the pods. The Deployment hasn't changed, so Kubernetes leaves them running with the old values. Force a restart with kubectl rollout restart deployment/frontend -n demo.

Also by design

nginx serves runtime-config.js with no-store, while hashed files under /assets/ are cached for a year as immutable. A cached config file would be the one thing capable of pointing a production browser at a dev API.

09  Inside the container

Dockerfile · nginx.conf · .dockerignore

The image is built in two stages. The first stage has Node, npm, the source and all the dependencies. The second stage takes only the compiled output from the first and puts it behind nginx. Everything used to build the app is discarded. 

# ---------- stage 1: build ----------
FROM node:22.12.0-alpine AS build
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci                      # cached unless the lockfile changes
COPY vite.config.js index.html ./
COPY src ./src
RUN npm run build

# ---------- stage 2: runtime ----------
FROM nginx:alpine AS runtime
COPY --from=build --chown=nginx:nginx /build/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
USER 101:101                   # unprivileged; never root
EXPOSE 3000                    # unprivileged port; no extra capability needed
HEALTHCHECK CMD wget --spider http://localhost:3000/healthz || exit 1

Why each choice is there

ChoiceReason
Multi-stage buildThe final image has no Node runtime, no node_modules and no source code — a much smaller image and far fewer things for Trivy to find.
Lockfile copied firstDocker caches layers. Changing a component doesn't re-download every dependency, so most builds take seconds instead of minutes.
USER 101:101If someone breaks out of the web server, they land as an unprivileged user, not root. Every path nginx writes to is relocated under /tmp to make this possible.
Port 3000, not 80Ports below 1024 need a special capability. Listening high means the container needs no elevated privilege at all.
/healthzA plain-text endpoint that answers without touching the filesystem and is excluded from access logs, used by the Docker healthcheck and both Kubernetes probes.
Alpine baseA few megabytes of OS instead of a few hundred — fewer packages, fewer CVEs.
.dockerignoreKeeps node_modules, .git, coverage/ and tests out of the build context. Faster, and no chance of a stray local file ending up in the image.
Security headersnginx always sends X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY and a strict Referrer-Policy; server_tokens off hides the version.
JSON access logsLogs come out structured, so they land in a log system in the same shape as every other service.

10  On the cluster

k8s/deployment.yaml · service.yaml · configmap.yaml

Three small YAML files describe the entire running system. Kubernetes reads them as a desired state and works continuously to make reality match — which is why a killed pod comes back without anyone being paged.

ObjectIts one jobKey settings here
Deployment Keep N copies of this image running, and replace them safely on update replicas: 1 · image: IMAGE_PLACEHOLDER · probes on /healthz · cpu 25m / mem 64Mi–192Mi
Service Give those pods one stable address inside the cluster port 80 → targetPort http (3000)
ConfigMap Hold non-secret settings, injected as environment variables API_BASE_URL · APP_ENV

Liveness vs readiness — the distinction that confuses everyone

  • Liveness asks "is this container still alive?" If it fails, Kubernetes restarts the container.
  • Readiness asks "can it serve traffic right now?" If it fails, Kubernetes removes the pod from the Service but leaves it running.

Readiness is what makes a zero-downtime rollout possible: a new pod receives no traffic until it says it is ready, and the old pod is only removed once the new one is.

What a rollout actually does

Known limits of this setup

replicas: 1 means there is no redundancy: during a restart there is a brief gap, and a node failure takes the site down until the pod is rescheduled. There is also no Ingress in these manifests, so the Service is reachable only from inside the cluster. Both are reasonable for a demo namespace and both are the first things to change for real traffic.

11  Run it locally

Node 20 or newer required

Develop

npm ci                      # install exactly what the lockfile says
npm run dev                 # http://localhost:5173

The dev server proxies /api to http://localhost:8080, so there is no CORS setup and no API host written into the code. Point it elsewhere with VITE_DEV_API_TARGET=http://some-host:8080 npm run dev.

Run the same checks CI runs

npm run lint                # must produce zero warnings
npm run test                # unit tests
npm run test:coverage       # tests + coverage/lcov.info
npm run build               # produces dist/
npm run preview             # serve the built bundle on :3000

Running these before you push is the cheapest way to avoid a red pipeline.

Build and run the real image

docker build -t frontend:local .

docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 \
  -e API_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8080 \
  -e APP_ENV=dev \
  frontend:local

# then check the two things the cluster checks:
curl -i http://localhost:3000/healthz
curl -s http://localhost:3000/runtime-config.js

The second command is the useful one — it shows you the exact file the entrypoint generated, which is where nine out of ten "the app can't reach the API" problems turn out to be.

Scan it the way the pipeline does

docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  aquasec/trivy:latest image --severity CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed frontend:local

12  Set it up yourself

One-time AWS and GitHub configuration — do it in this order

If you are wiring this pipeline to a fresh AWS account, these are the six steps. Steps 2 and 3 are the ones that replace an access key, so take them slowly.

1 — Create the ECR repository

aws ecr create-repository \
  --repository-name ai-interview-dev-platform/frontend \
  --region ap-south-1 \
  --image-scanning-configuration scanOnPush=true

2 — Register GitHub as an identity provider (once per AWS account)

aws iam create-open-id-connect-provider \
  --url https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  --client-id-list sts.amazonaws.com

This is what tells AWS "tokens signed by GitHub are worth reading". It grants nothing on its own — permission still comes entirely from the next step.

3 — Create the role with its trust policy

Save the trust policy from section 04 as trust.json, replacing <ACCOUNT_ID> and the repository name, then: 

aws iam create-role \
  --role-name gh-deploy-frontend \
  --assume-role-policy-document file://trust.json

aws iam put-role-policy \
  --role-name gh-deploy-frontend \
  --policy-name deploy-permissions \
  --policy-document file://permissions.json   # from section 07
Check before you continue

Open the trust policy once more and confirm the sub is the full, exact string — and that it uses the environment:production form, because the deploy job declares an environment. A wildcard here is the difference between "only my pipeline" and "anyone on GitHub".

4 — Let the role into the cluster

Run the two access-entry commands from section 07. Then verify:

aws eks list-access-entries --cluster-name ai-interview
kubectl create namespace demo   # if it doesn't exist yet

5 — Add the GitHub configuration

WhereNameValue
Settings → Environmentsproductioncreate it; add required reviewers if you want a human approval before deploys
Environment secretsAWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARNarn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:role/gh-deploy-frontend
Repository secretsSONAR_TOKENfrom SonarCloud → My Account → Security

Adjust the four values at the top of ci.yml — AWS_REGION, EKS_CLUSTER, K8S_NAMESPACE, ECR_REPO — and the two keys in sonar-project.properties, to match your own account.

6 — Try it

Use Actions → CI/CD frontend → Run workflow for the first attempt rather than pushing. It exercises the identical path but on your schedule, and the "Check config" step will tell you immediately if a secret is missing.

One inconsistency to be aware of

The workflow triggers on both main and master, but the deploy job only runs when the ref is refs/heads/master. On a repository whose default branch is main, all the checks will run and the deploy will be silently skipped. If that is not what you want, change the if: condition in the deploy job to match your branch.

13  When it breaks

The failures you will actually meet, and what causes them

Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity

Almost always the trust policy. In order of likelihood:

1. The sub uses the branch form …:ref:refs/heads/master but the job declares environment: production, so GitHub actually sent …:environment:production. 2. The repository owner or name is misspelled — it is case-sensitive. 3. The OIDC provider was never created in this account. 4. The aud is not sts.amazonaws.com.

To see the real subject, add a step that prints ${{ github.repository }} and the event, and compare with the trust policy character by character.

Credentials could not be loaded / no OIDC token available

The job is missing permissions: id-token: write. Job-level permissions replace the workflow default entirely, so if you add a permissions: block to a job you must list every permission that job needs, including contents: read.

The pod is stuck in ImagePullBackOff

Either the sed did not substitute the image (the pod is literally trying to pull IMAGE_PLACEHOLDER — the pipeline's grep guard exists to catch exactly this), or the cluster's node role lacks AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly and cannot pull from ECR. Check with kubectl describe pod -n demo -l app=frontend and read the events at the bottom.

rollout status timed out after 5 minutes

The new pod never became ready. Usually the readiness probe: nginx is not answering /healthz on port 3000, or the container crashed at start. Look at kubectl logs -n demo -l app=frontend --tail=50. The pipeline has already rolled back by the time you read this, so the site is fine — you are debugging the new image, not an outage.

Trivy fails the build on a CRITICAL vulnerability

This is the gate working. Fix it by bumping the base image in the Dockerfile (node:…-alpine and nginx:…-alpine) or the offending npm package, then push again. Resist adding an ignore file as the first move — if you must, record why and set an expiry date.

Gitleaks found a secret

Removing the line and committing again will not help: the old commit still contains it and Gitleaks reads the whole history. Treat the secret as compromised and rotate it first — that is the part that actually protects you. Only then rewrite history (git filter-repo) if you need the scan to pass.

Login fails with "the server returned a web page instead of data"

Expected in the demo namespace as it stands. API_BASE_URL is empty, meaning same-origin, but nothing routes /api to a backend yet — so nginx answers with the SPA fallback (index.html, HTTP 200) and the app receives HTML where it expected JSON. Add an Ingress that routes /api to the middleware, or point API_BASE_URL at a reachable API.

I changed the ConfigMap and nothing happened

Correct behaviour, not a bug. The Deployment is unchanged, so Kubernetes has nothing to do. Run kubectl rollout restart deployment/frontend -n demo.

Useful commands when you are stuck 
kubectl get pods -n demo -l app=frontend
kubectl describe pod -n demo -l app=frontend
kubectl logs -n demo -l app=frontend --tail=100
kubectl get deploy frontend -n demo -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'
kubectl rollout history deployment/frontend -n demo
kubectl port-forward -n demo svc/frontend 8081:80    # then open localhost:8081

14  Glossary

Every term on this page, in one place

Action
A reusable step someone else published, referenced by name and version, e.g. actions/checkout@v4.
Artifact
Something a build produces. Here: the dist/ folder, and the container image.
ARN
Amazon Resource Name — the unique identifier of any AWS thing.
aud (audience)
The claim in a token saying who it is meant for. Must be sts.amazonaws.com so a token issued for something else cannot be replayed at AWS.
CI / CD
Continuous Integration (build and test every change) / Continuous Deployment (ship it automatically when the checks pass).
Claim
A statement inside a token — who issued it, who it is for, which repository and branch it came from.
ConfigMap
A Kubernetes object holding non-secret settings as key/value pairs.
Container
A running instance of an image, isolated from the host.
CVE
A publicly catalogued vulnerability with an ID like CVE-2024-1234. What Trivy looks for.
Deployment
The Kubernetes object that keeps N copies of a pod running and replaces them safely on update.
Digest
The cryptographic hash of an image's exact contents. Two identical digests are the same bytes.
ECR
Elastic Container Registry — AWS's private image storage.
EKS
Elastic Kubernetes Service — Kubernetes with the control plane run by AWS.
Environment
A named GitHub deployment target that can hold its own secrets and require approval before a job runs.
IAM
Identity and Access Management — AWS's system for who may do what.
Image
A sealed, layered filesystem plus a start command. Runs the same everywhere.
Ingress
The Kubernetes object that exposes services to the outside world and routes by hostname and path. Not present in this repo yet.
Job
A group of steps in a workflow that runs on one machine. Jobs run in parallel unless linked by needs.
JWT
JSON Web Token — a signed block of claims. The OIDC token is one.
Lockfile
package-lock.json: the exact version of every dependency and sub-dependency. What makes builds reproducible.
Least privilege
Granting the minimum permissions needed for the job and nothing more.
Manifest
A YAML file describing a Kubernetes object.
Namespace
A named partition inside a cluster. This app lives in demo.
OIDC
OpenID Connect — the standard that lets one system prove its identity to another using a signed, expiring token instead of a shared password.
Pod
The smallest unit Kubernetes runs: one or more containers sharing an address and lifecycle.
Probe
A periodic health check. Liveness restarts a sick container; readiness withholds traffic from one that isn't ready.
ReplicaSet
The object a Deployment creates to hold one specific version of a pod. Rollback means switching back to the previous one.
Rollback
Returning to the previously working version. Here: kubectl rollout undo, run automatically on failure.
Runner
The temporary virtual machine GitHub Actions runs a job on. Created fresh, destroyed after.
Secret
In GitHub: an encrypted value exposed to workflows and masked in logs. In Kubernetes: an object for sensitive values — not used by this frontend, which has nothing secret.
Service
A stable in-cluster address that load-balances across the pods matching its selector.
SHA
The 40-character hash identifying a git commit. Used here as the image tag.
SPA fallback
Serving index.html for any unknown path so client-side routing works on a page refresh.
STS
Security Token Service — the AWS service that issues temporary credentials.
sub (subject)
The claim saying who a token is about. For GitHub Actions it encodes the repository plus the branch or environment. The single most important line in the trust policy.
Trust policy
The rule on an IAM role saying who is allowed to assume it, and under what conditions.
Workflow
A YAML file under .github/workflows/ describing when to run jobs and what they do.
Generated from the repository itself — .github/workflows/ci.yml, Dockerfile, nginx.conf, k8s/, vite.config.js.
If the pipeline changes, change this page too.
